issues.description: The Procedures section states that participants chose their own conditions. Self-selection into experimental conditions destroys random assignment, introduces selection confounds, and makes any between-condition comparison uninterpretable as causal. This also directly contradicts the Overview, which states participants were randomly assigned. If this is literally what the Qualtrics flow does, it is a fatal design flaw; if it is a writing error it still must be corrected because it defines the core internal validity of the study.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The Overview describes random assignment to conditions, but the Procedures section says participants selected their preferred conditions. These statements are mutually exclusive and the reader cannot determine how participants actually entered conditions, which is essential for evaluating validity.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to three conditions, with two groups acquiring information about statistical or identifiable victims respectively.

issues.description: The Design section labels the study a within-subject design, but the descriptive tables report different and non-overlapping sample sizes for each cell (e.g., 159, 175, 166), the analyses are two-way ANOVAs with a large residual df (994) consistent with between-subjects comparisons, and the original studies were between-subjects. Calling this a within-subject design is incorrect and would imply a completely different (and inappropriate) error structure for the reported tests.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: The post-hoc interpretation states that statistical-victim participants donated more (M=2.54) than identifiable-victim participants (M=2.24). However, the descriptive statistics in Table 7 show the identifiable condition means (2.58 and 2.50) are higher than the statistical condition means (2.46 and 2.01). The means appear swapped/mislabeled, and the verbal conclusion (statistical > identifiable) is the opposite of what the descriptive data show and the opposite of Hypothesis 1. This is a substantive inconsistency that reverses the central finding.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: Significant p-value with effect-size CI spanning zero
issues.description: Several post-hoc comparisons are flagged as significant (p<.05) yet report effect-size 95% confidence intervals that include zero. A standardized effect size CI that contains 0 is logically inconsistent with a significant difference at the same alpha, indicating either the CI was computed on a different scale/method than the test or one of the values is erroneous. As presented they cannot both be correct.

issues.subcategory: Significant p-value with effect-size CI spanning zero (extension)
issues.description: The extension's only 'significant' contrast (statistical vs. joint, p=.041) reports d=0.08 with a 95% CI of [-0.07, 0.23] that includes zero. This contradiction between the p-value and the interval undermines the headline extension claim and must be resolved.

The abstract claims support for lower perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim or an identifiable-victim-with-statistics. But Hypothesis 6 predicted the identifiable victim would elicit HIGHER perceived impact than statistical victims, and the actual result (Table 14) shows only a statistical-vs-joint difference (statistical higher than joint), with identifiable-vs-statistical non-significant. The abstract therefore misrepresents both the hypothesis direction and the obtained pattern.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Uncorrected multiple comparisons across feeling items
issues.description: Table 13 reports 18 F-tests across six segregated-feeling outcomes by three effects, with no family-wise correction. The single 'significant' result (perceived impact, p=.045) is borderline and emerges from a large family of tests run on a random/dummy dataset, making it almost certainly a false positive. Treating this as confirmatory support for the extension is inappropriate without correction or pre-specified focus.

issues.subcategory: Dropping the original's censored-data model (ordered probit)
issues.description: The original study analyzed donations (bounded 0–5, heavily censored at the endpoints) with ordered probit regression. The replication explicitly drops this analysis and relies solely on ANOVA, which assumes interval, approximately normal, homoscedastic outcomes that a censored 0–5 donation variable typically violates. Omitting the censored-data model both deviates from the original analytic approach and risks biased/inefficient estimates, weakening the replication comparison.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The original measured actual donation of real money the participant possessed; the replication uses a purely hypothetical indication of how much one 'would donate' with no real money or endowment. Hypothetical giving may not engage the same affective/deliberative processes underlying the identifiable victim effect, so the DV may not operationalize the same construct, threatening the validity of the replication test even though the change is disclosed.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Power analysis details absent from main text
issues.description: The manuscript asserts the sample was determined to ensure adequate power but provides no target effect size, alpha, power, or resulting N in the main text—only a circular statement and a pointer to supplementary material. Readers cannot evaluate whether the study is adequately powered (especially given the very small original/meta-analytic effects, e.g., d=0.23 in Study 3 and a meta-analytic mean of 0.05) without these numbers.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study.

issues.description: Participants with prior knowledge of the effect and those failing the attention check are said to be excluded, but no counts are given and analyses appear to use the full N=1000. The number excluded, the resulting analyzed N per cell, and whether exclusions differ across conditions are needed to evaluate bias and to reproduce the analyses.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The analysis combines several distinct emotional/cognitive items (upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and—in the extension—perceived impact) into a single 'aggregated feelings' score, but no internal-consistency statistic (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) or factor justification is provided. Without evidence the items form a coherent construct, the aggregate measure's validity is unestablished, and including 'perceived impact' both as an extension item and in the aggregate is potentially circular.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: Availability heuristic vs. affect heuristic conflation
issues.description: The introduction attributes the affective response to identifiable victims to the 'availability heuristic,' but the mechanism described (stronger affect/sympathy driving valuation) corresponds to the affect heuristic emphasized by Slovic and by Small & Loewenstein, and reflected in the keyword 'affective heuristics.' Misattributing the mechanism to availability (ease of retrieval from memory) reflects a conceptual mislabeling of the theoretical framework.
issues.quote: The “availability heuristic”  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.subcategory: MTurk sample vs. broad human-tendency claims
issues.description: The framing repeatedly describes the effect as a general 'human tendency,' yet the original was a Pennsylvania lab/student-center sample and the replication uses MTurk workers; neither supports broad cross-population generalization. The change in population (a contextual variable) may itself moderate the effect, and this limitation is not adequately reconciled with the universal language used.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is the human’s tendency to offer greater support to an identifiable individual over a larger group of anonymous victims represented by numerical statistics

issues.subcategory: Implausible simulated demographics undermine placeholder validity
issues.description: The placeholder dataset reports a mean age of 67.8 (SD=30.1) with a range of 18–120 and median 68 for an MTurk sample—demographically implausible (e.g., age 120; mean far above typical MTurk). While disclaimed as simulated, such values signal the dummy data may not reflect realistic distributions, limiting the usefulness of the simulated method/results sections for anticipating real analyses and assumption checks.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: Original study N vs. reported degrees of freedom
issues.description: Study 1 is reported as N=121, but the ANOVA residual df is given as 115 (Table 1) while the contrast t-test for the same study uses df=117 (Table 11). A 2x2 ANOVA on N=121 would have error df=117, not 115, and the two tables disagree with each other. These discrepancies suggest transcription errors in summarizing the original statistics used as the replication benchmark.
issues.quote: Effect of identifiability and intervention on donation (Study 1) (N=121)

issues.subcategory: Correlational feelings–donation link framed as predictive
issues.description: The feelings–donation relationship is assessed with simple Pearson correlations within conditions yet described in predictive/explanatory terms ('whether affective feelings predict donation'). With no temporal/mediational design or control for confounds, and feelings measured after donation, causal or predictive language overstates what correlational, post-hoc associations can support.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: Merging Study 1 (2x2 identifiable/statistical × intervention) and Study 3 (3-level identifiability, no intervention) into a single 3×2 design, and newly applying the intervention to the joint condition that the original never manipulated, changes the factorial structure and the meaning of the interaction tests. The 'identifiable but not statistical' interaction prediction becomes ambiguous with three identifiability levels, and the added joint×intervention cells are not anchored to any original finding, complicating interpretation of replication success/failure.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.
